title: Presentations & vivas
examples: How do I structure a 15-minute presentation?
What should I do if I don't know the answer during a viva?
Can you give me tips for managing presentation nerves?

explain.say: A good presentation needs a clear structure to guide your audience.

items: Body: Present main arguments and evidence

explain.say: The introduction must grab attention and clearly state your main purpose.
The body paragraphs need strong evidence to support your core ideas.
Always end with a conclusion that neatly wraps up your main points.
When handling questions in a viva, listen carefully before answering anything.
A real-life example is defending your final year project in front of experts.

faq.q: How long should my presentation be for a first-year university module?
faq.a: Typically, check the module handbook for specific time limits. Most undergraduate presentations range from ten to fifteen minutes.
asks: Should I aim for ten minutes?

faq.q: If I do not know the answer to a question, should I guess?
faq.a: It is better to admit you do not know something than to guess incorrectly. You can say you need to look into it further.
asks: Is it okay to say I don't know?

faq.q: Should I read directly from my slides during the presentation?
faq.a: No, your slides should guide you, not replace you. Use them as prompts and speak conversationally to your audience.
asks: How much talking is too much?

faq.q: What is the difference between a presentation and a viva voce?
faq.a: A presentation is your guided talk, while the viva is a more spontaneous questioning session about your work.
asks: What is the purpose of the viva?

faq.q: How can I make my conclusion memorable for the marker?
faq.a: End with a strong, forward-looking statement about the implications of your research. This shows depth of thought.

facts: A strong structure helps the audience follow your line of reasoning.
When answering questions, pause to gather your thoughts before speaking.
The introduction must clearly state the presentation's main aim.
A conclusion should summarise, not introduce, new material.

quiz.say: Which element is most crucial for structuring the main body of your talk?

options.show: The analysis that links evidence back to your main thesis.
options.say: The analysis that links evidence back to your main thesis.

options.show: Listing all the data points you found.
options.say: Listing all the data points you found.

options.show: Spending too much time on the introduction.
options.say: Spending too much time on the introduction.

quiz.why: The analysis is where you show why the evidence matters, which is the core academic skill.

wrong.1: This only shows information, but not your understanding of it.
wrong.2: Overly complex words can confuse the audience, making your points unclear.
wrong.3: While important, the body needs the most time to demonstrate your research.

quiz.say: When a marker asks a question you are unsure about, what is the best immediate action?

options.show: Saying you need a moment to consider the question.
options.say: Saying you need a moment to consider the question.

options.show: Giving a very short, unelaborated answer.
options.say: Giving a very short, unelaborated answer.

quiz.why: Buying time with a thoughtful pause makes you appear composed and thoughtful.

wrong.1: This can make you seem nervous or unprepared.
wrong.2: This avoids the question but shows you cannot handle pressure.
wrong.3: A short answer suggests you haven't fully processed the depth of the question.

quiz.say: If your presentation is about the causes of World War One, what should the conclusion focus on?

options.show: Simply repeating the three causes you listed.
options.say: Simply repeating the three causes you listed.

options.show: Introducing a fourth cause you forgot to mention.
options.say: Introducing a fourth cause you forgot to mention.

options.show: Apologizing for any weaknesses in your research.
options.say: Apologizing for any weaknesses in your research.

options.show: The long-term impact of the war on international relations.
options.say: The long-term impact of the war on international relations.

quiz.why: A strong conclusion looks beyond the scope of the presentation to show broader significance.

wrong.0: This is just summarizing, not concluding with a broader insight.
wrong.1: Never introduce new material in the conclusion; it confuses the audience.
wrong.2: This undermines your confidence and the perceived quality of your work.
